verses.text: The sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel (for he was the firstborn; but, because he defiled his father’s couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph the son of Israel; and the genealogy is not to be listed according to the birthright.
For Judah prevailed above his brothers, and from him came the prince; but the birthright was Joseph’s) —
the sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
The sons of Joel: Shemaiah his son, Gog his son, Shimei his son,
Micah his son, Reaiah his son, Baal his son,
and Beerah his son, whom Tilgath Pilneser king of Assyria carried away captive. He was prince of the Reubenites.
His brothers by their families, when the genealogy of their generations was listed: the chief, Jeiel, and Zechariah,
and Bela the son of Azaz, the son of Shema, the son of Joel, who lived in Aroer, even to Nebo and Baal Meon;
and he lived eastward even to the entrance of the wilderness from the river Euphrates, because their livestock were multiplied in the land of Gilead.
In the days of Saul, they made war with the Hagrites, who fell by their hand; and they lived in their tents throughout all the land east of Gilead.
The sons of Gad lived over against them, in the land of Bashan to Salecah:
Joel the chief, Shapham the second, Janai, and Shaphat in Bashan.
Their brothers of their fathers’ houses: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia, and Eber, seven.
These were the sons of Abihail, the son of Huri, the son of Jaroah, the son of Gilead, the son of Michael, the son of Jeshishai, the son of Jahdo, the son of Buz;
Ahi the son of Abdiel, the son of Guni, chief of their fathers’ houses.
They lived in Gilead in Bashan, and in its towns, and in all the suburbs of Sharon, as far as their borders.
All these were listed by genealogies in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel.

The sons of Reuben, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, of valiant men, men able to bear buckler and sword, and to shoot with bow, and skillful in war, were forty-four thousand seven hundred sixty, that were able to go out to war.
They made war with the Hagrites, with Jetur, and Naphish, and Nodab.

They were helped against them, and the Hagrites were delivered into their hand, and all who were with them; for they cried to God in the battle, and he was answered them, because they put their trust in him.
They took away their livestock; of their camels fifty thousand, and of sheep two hundred fifty thousand, and of donkeys two thousand, and of men one hundred thousand.
For many fell slain, because the war was of God. They lived in their place until the captivity.
The children of the half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land: they increased from Bashan to Baal Hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon.
These were the heads of their fathers’ houses: even Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty men of valor, famous men, heads of their fathers’ houses.
They trespassed against the God of their fathers, and played the prostitute after the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God destroyed before them.

So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgath Pilneser king of Assyria, and he carried them away, even the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and brought them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and to the river of Gozan, to this day.

footnotes.content: Here the scribe must tell an old, hard story: Reuben was born first, yet his own sin cost him what birthright means. Even a father's love cannot paper over that loss. Watch how the Lord honors faithfulness, not mere birth order.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah rose, and Joseph kept the birthright Reuben lost—yet the prince came from Judah's line. This is how the Lord works: He lifts up the faithful and weaves their place into His story, even when they started far behind.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four sons named: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, Carmi—each a branch holding Reuben's name into the future. Names matter; generations matter. The Lord does not let faithfulness fade into silence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joel's line held the family priesthood through David's day. One name echoes down through a dozen: son, grandson, great-grandson—a ladder reaching from Joel all the way to Shemaiah. That's how God builds a people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Micah, Reaiah, Baal—names strung together like beads on a thread, each one a person, each one known. The scribe takes time to honor them. So does the Lord, even names the world forgets.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beerah was prince of Reuben when the Assyrian king dragged him away to captivity. A name spoken for all time, not to glorify him, but so the captivity is remembered—and so we remember that exile is real, and so is the faithfulness of those who faced it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeiel and Zechariah were chieftains when the genealogy was reckoned. The scribe names them so history will know: these men held their tribes together, kept the records, guarded the memory of who they were.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bela lived in Aroer, a real place east of the Jordan—from Nebo to Baal Meon, names on a map. The Lord knows where His people dwell, down to each town and well, just as He knows where you rest tonight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They had room to spread—pasture reaching to the Euphrates itself. When God gives room, He gives it for a reason: to flourish, to multiply, to see His faithfulness overflow into generations. Gratitude is the only right answer to such plenty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Saul was king, the Reubenites fought the Hagrites and won—not because they were mightiest, but because they trusted. The Lord fights for those who call to Him first, before they fight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gad's sons camped across from Reuben, in Bashan's pastures all the way to Salecah. They lived facing one another, tribes in covenant, land held together in mutual trust. That's how God means for His people to dwell.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joel, the chief; Shapham second; Janai and Shaphat below them—a chain of command, clear and humble. Leadership is not vanity; it's the willingness to serve a people faithfully and know your place in the line.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven brothers of their father's house, all named. Not one lost in the crowd. The scribe honors each: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia, Eber. Our God is a God of particulars, and so are His servants.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One long line of descent: father, grandfather, great-grandfather—Abihail, Huri, Jaroah, Gilead, Michael, Jeshishai, Jahdo, Buz, each one a link in the chain holding the people together across time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahi was chief of their fathers' houses—the one who kept the trust, the one they came to when hard choices loomed. A faithful elder is worth more than gold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gilead in Bashan, its towns and the suburbs of Sharon—the geography is exact, named so no one would forget. The Lord's people live in a real land, with real places where He has put them down and called them home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jotham and Jeroboam—kings from a later age—verified the genealogy themselves. When rulers can say 'these records are true, these people are who they claim,' you know the record is weighty and the lineage real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty-four thousand warriors, able to fight with bow and sword—the Lord counts them all. But number alone doesn't win wars; faith does. The number is recorded so we will see that even great strength serves under the Lord's command.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: War with the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, Nodab—foes with real names, real plans. The Lord does not hide that His people faced enemies. He teaches us that faith is not escape from struggle, but trust through it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They cried to God in battle, and He answered—the Hagrites fell. This is the Lord's pattern: when we call on Him, He hears, and He delivers. Not always without cost, but always faithfully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fifty thousand camels, two hundred fifty thousand sheep, two thousand donkeys—the spoils of victory, listed exactly. The Lord is not stingy with His blessings to those who trust Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Many fell, the war was of God—victory came not from might alone, but from the Lord's hand. Yet after, they rested in their place until captivity came. Even the victorious cannot escape exile if they turn from the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Half of Manasseh spread from Bashan to the high places—Baal Hermon, Senir, Mount Hermon, reaching to heaven itself. The Lord gave them room to grow, and they did, from one place to many.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven mighty men, famous for valor, heads of their houses—Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, Jahdiel. A good name is better than great wealth, and the Lord remembers the righteous.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They played the prostitute after the gods of the peoples—a pattern we still hear echoed today. Readers in any age know the seduction of belonging to the world around us, the slow drift away from what we once held true. The Lord still calls us back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pul and Tilgath Pilneser carried them away—real kings, real exile, real loss. The Lord did not hide their failure or soften the cost. But He did not lose them either. Even in Gozan, He knew where they were.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
